item.title: Adult ADHD, Stimulants, and Psychosis
item.description:
ADHD

Adult ADHD, Stimulants, and Psychosis

As more adults use prescription stimulants, cases of psychosis may increase.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • In the US, prescription stimulant use is on the rise, mostly due to adult usage.
  • This reflects an increase in ADHD, whether due to changes in diagnostic criteria or over-diagnosis.
  • Although psychosis with prescription stimulants is rare, the risk may increase as more adults use them.
Source: Davie Bicker / Pixabay

The use of prescription stimulants like Ritalin (methylphenidate), Adderall (mixed amphetamine/dextroamphetamine), Dexadrine (dextroamphetamine), and Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine), ostensibly to treat attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), has shot up over the past two decades here in the US, an increase driven mostly by adults. From 2005 to 2019, the number of US adults prescribed stimulants increased fivefold, and during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, prescriptions increased another 10% among women 15- to 49-year-old and men 25 to 49 years old.1 As of the past few years, that amounts to as many as 4% of commercially insured US adults taking prescription stimulants.

Adult ADHD Is on the Rise

Why the increase? Part of the answer is that the diagnosis of adult ADHD has also gone up over the past two decades, though how to explain that has been debated going back years without clear resolution.

As with rising rates of autism, it could be that the detection of adult ADHD has gone up due to loosened diagnostic criteria for ADHD in the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) published in 2013, clinicians increasingly diagnosing the condition on the “soft” end of the illness spectrum, and greater public awareness and destigmatization of the diagnosis thanks to social media. It’s also possible that the biological effects of COVID-19 and the fact that many of us are increasingly living our lives online are taxing our brains at home and work like never before, taking a toll on our ability to focus and making it increasingly obvious that human brains aren’t particularly good at multitasking.3 Notably, about half of US adults with ADHD were diagnosed as adults, even though the DSM-5 diagnosis requires symptom onset before the age of 12.3

It could also be that ADHD is increasingly “over-diagnosed,” a longstanding claim that has been rekindled of late by Robert F. Kennedy Jr’s Make America Health Again (MAHA) Commission. In certain sectors like finance and the tech industry, employees often work long hours and view stimulants as a way to make it through the day, pull all-nighters, and keep up or compete with co-workers who take them.4 Other people may be engaging in inaccurate self-diagnosis due to the popularity of ADHD on social media where misinformation about and misrepresentations of the disorder abound.5

All of these explanations have some teeth and are by no means mutually exclusive. ADHD may be accurately diagnosed in an increasing number of adults, underdiagnosed (e.g., among women and minority groups) or untreated (only about a third of people with a diagnosis of ADHD report receiving treatment in the past year) in others, and overdiagnosed in still others.

Obtaining Prescription Stimulants Is Easier Than Ever

Diagnosis aside, the increase in stimulant use for ADHD reflects how little effort it can take to obtain a prescription these days, especially here in the US, which consumes some 68% of the world’s prescription stimulants.6 For individuals who are distracted or forgetful; struggle with attention, organization, and multi-tasking; don’t always pay attention to what people are saying; and find themselves being forgetful or losing things—symptoms that almost all of us experience from time to time—it’s easy to get a stimulant prescription by filling out an online questionnaire, seeing a mental health provider via telepsychiatry (note that one of the sharpest rise of stimulant prescriptions in recent years has been by nurse practitioners7), and “doctor shopping” when they get turned down.

Unlike some medications, stimulants tend to sharpen focus regardless of whether someone has ADHD or not so that people seek them out and psychiatrists end up prescribing them for what amounts to “neuroenhancement,” similar to the use of performance-enhancing drugs (PESs) like anabolic steroids to enhance physical performance.8 Others—including as many as 46% of college students in one study—obtain stimulant medications without a prescription or an ADHD diagnosis, noting that they help to “stay awake longer, have a more enjoyable time, and to party longer.”9

More Stimulants, More Psychosis Risk

The potential upsides of receiving prescription stimulants for properly diagnosed ADHD include associations with lower mortality, suicidal behavior, substance misuse, and criminality.10,11 Meanwhile, rates of prescription stimulant misuse have decreased to just 1.9% of US adults in recent years.12 So why fret about growing rates of prescription stimulants?

One reason to worry is that even supervised prescription use can result in side effects. Although previous studies have yielded mixed results, a 2024 case-control study found that long-term exposure to stimulants for ADHD was associated with greater risks of cardiovascular disease, especially high blood pressure and arterial disease.13

And then there’s the psychosis risk. It's been well-known since at least the 1950s that illicit or recreational stimulant use of drugs like methamphetamine can cause an acute, florid psychosis. Recreational use also substantially increases the risk of first-episode psychosis.

The risk of psychosis with prescription stimulants taken at appropriate doses is much, much less but it’s not zero.14 A 2019 study found that the rate of new onset psychosis with prescription medications in a sample of adolescents and young adults was 1 in 660 patients.15 With some 2 million patients taking prescription amphetamines, that amounts to thousands of patients. A more recent case-control study also found that the chance of developing psychosis or mania was greater among those taking prescription stimulants than not with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.68.16 For high doses of prescription stimulants—more than 30 mg/day dextroamphetamine equivalents (i.e., 40 mg of Adderall and 100 mg of Vyvanse)—the risk of psychosis or mania was 5.3 greater compared to those not on stimulants with an attributable risk percentage of 81%.

These days, I see a lot of patients hospitalized with psychosis who are taking prescription stimulants as outpatients. Association isn’t causation, so this could just reflect the fact that so many adults are now on stimulants—perhaps especially in the Bay Area where I work. But it’s always possible that the stimulants are worsening the psychosis or are being taken at non-prescribed doses, very likely that they’ll interfere with the effectiveness of antipsychotic medications, and uncertain—in the midst of hospitalization for psychosis—whether a patient really has ADHD or not. As a general rule, stimulants are therefore held, at least during the hospitalization and until resolution of psychosis.

The Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) is deliberating whether and when to reinstate a previous law that required in-person visits for controlled substances including prescription stimulants. That law was suspended during COVID-19 to prevent people with ADHD from running out of medications, but the post-COVID spike in prescriptions for adult ADHD may result in its reinstatement sooner rather than later.

item.title: Back-to-School Tips Every Parent Needs for a Successful School Year
item.description:
Parenting

Back-to-School Tips Every Parent Needs for a Successful School Year

Practical parenting tips to reduce stress and build school success.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Preparing children emotionally is just as important as buying school supplies.
  • Teaching digital responsibility helps children use school technology safely and wisely.
  • Viewing behavior as communication can help parents respond with empathy instead of punishment.

As summer winds down, many parents find themselves preparing for another school year by shopping for backpacks, filling out paperwork, and checking supply lists. While those tasks are important, the most valuable preparation comes from helping children feel emotionally, physically, and mentally ready for the transition.

The shift from carefree summer days to structured school routines is a significant adjustment for children of all ages. New teachers, unfamiliar classmates, earlier mornings, academic expectations, and changing social dynamics can leave even confident children feeling overwhelmed. Fortunately, a few intentional strategies can make the transition smoother while setting the stage for a successful year.

Prioritize Sleep Before School Starts

One of the biggest challenges families face each August is resetting sleep schedules after weeks of later bedtimes and slower mornings. Unfortunately, waiting until the night before school starts often leads to exhausted children and stressful mornings.

Sleep is essential for attention, learning, emotional regulation, memory, and physical health. Children who are sleep deprived are more likely to struggle with irritability, anxiety, behavioral concerns, and difficulty concentrating in the classroom.

Rather than making an abrupt change, begin shifting bedtime and wake-up time approximately three weeks before school begins. Moving each by just 15 to 20 minutes every few days allows the body's internal clock to adjust more naturally.

Parents can also improve sleep hygiene by establishing a predictable bedtime routine, limiting screens during the hour before bed, and encouraging children to spend time outside in the morning. Exposure to natural light shortly after waking helps regulate circadian rhythms, making it easier to fall asleep the following evening.

Older children will resist these changes. They may try to sneak electronic devices into their bedroom. They may try to negotiate with you. They may argue and tell you that they can stay up late and still wake up on time for school. Make these changes anyway.

Recognize That Back-to-School Anxiety Is Normal

Even children who enjoy school often experience anxiety before the first day. Think about it from a child's perspective. They may be entering a classroom where they know few people, are navigating unfamiliar routines, wondering if they'll like their teacher, or worrying about fitting in socially. That's a tremendous amount of uncertainty for a developing brain.

Parents can reduce anxiety by acknowledging these feelings rather than dismissing them. Statements like, "It's okay to feel nervous about something new," help children understand that anxiety is a normal response to change—not a sign that something is wrong.

If your child is starting at a new school, visiting the building beforehand can be especially helpful. Walking through the hallways, locating classrooms, finding the cafeteria, and practicing the route to school all create familiarity that reduces uncertainty on the first day.

Build Independence Before the School Year Begins

Back-to-school season offers an excellent opportunity to gradually increase age-appropriate independence:

  • Preschoolers can practice opening lunch containers, putting on backpacks, and using the bathroom independently.
  • Elementary-aged children can begin packing their own backpacks, checking homework folders, and taking responsibility for simple morning routines.
  • Teenagers benefit from managing long-term assignments, communicating respectfully with teachers, and organizing their own schedules.

Allowing children to practice these skills before school begins builds confidence while reducing the number of reminders parents need to provide each morning.

Talk About School-Issued Technology

Many students now receive laptops or tablets from their schools. While these devices are valuable educational tools, they also require ongoing conversations about digital responsibility.

Children should understand that school-issued devices belong to the school—not to them. Activity completed on these devices may be monitored, and deleted content may not truly disappear. Teaching children to treat school technology professionally helps establish healthy digital habits that will benefit them throughout adulthood.

Parents should also review basic internet safety before school begins. Remind children never to share personal information online, click unfamiliar links, or communicate privately with strangers. Encourage them to tell a trusted adult immediately if something online makes them uncomfortable.

These conversations should focus on guidance. The goal is to help children develop good judgment—not simply avoid punishment.

Create Mornings That Feel Calm

The most successful morning routines begin the night before.

Simple habits like laying out clothes, packing backpacks, charging devices, filling water bottles, and reviewing the next day's schedule can dramatically reduce morning chaos. Visual checklists are especially helpful for younger children because they encourage independence while reducing repeated verbal reminders. When children know what to expect, mornings become less about rushing and more about starting the day with confidence.

Protect What Matters Most

Parents often feel pressure to enroll children in multiple extracurricular activities as the school year begins. While sports, music, and clubs offer wonderful opportunities, overscheduling can leave children chronically tired and emotionally overwhelmed. Children need unstructured time to relax, play, connect with family, and simply recover from the demands of the school day. Protecting adequate sleep, regular family meetings, and downtime is just as important as building an impressive résumé.

Know When to Seek Additional Support

Some nervousness during the first few weeks of school is completely expected.

However, persistent school refusal, panic attacks, ongoing sleep disturbances, frequent physical complaints without a medical explanation, significant mood changes, or a sudden decline in academic performance deserve further attention.

Children often communicate distress through behavior long before they can explain it with words. Viewing behavior as communication allows parents to respond with curiosity rather than punishment.

Back-to-school success isn't measured by perfect grades or flawless routines. Instead, it begins with helping children feel emotionally safe, well-rested, and confident enough to learn. As parents, we can't eliminate every challenge our children will encounter this school year. We can, however, provide the steady support that helps them navigate those challenges with resilience.

Preparing children for school is all about strengthening the skills they'll carry with them long after the school year ends.

item.title: When a Dream Becomes a Delusion
item.description:
Career

When a Dream Becomes a Delusion

Our culture worships hustling, but relentless pursuit can break hearts.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Career grief, the pain of unfulfilled ambition, is real and deserves to be taken seriously.
  • Our culture insists you keep trying until you succeed, but that message can quietly break people.
  • Early promise can be a curse. Sometimes the most gifted people fall the hardest.
Success comes at a price
Source: razihusin / Istockphoto

If at first you don't succeed, try, try, try again… Never give up on your dreams… you've got to have a dream; if you don't have a dream, how ya gonna have a dream come true?

The idea of striving valiantly toward success is so baked into our Western culture that it's almost a religion. Movies, books, and songs have been written about the heroes of our time who have struggled against adversity and come out on top. They started with nothing and made it big. Madonna arrived in New York in the '80s with only 20 bucks to her name and became the biggest superstar in the world; Oprah rose from humble beginnings to become the media titan of our age; Dolly Parton was so poor she wrote songs about her homemade coat of many colours. But it was all good because there's a cheerful ending to the story and they all lived happily ever after.

But what about the stories we never hear because no one wants to tell them? What about the majority of people who struck out for glory and fell short? In trying to write this post, it was nearly impossible to get anyone to open up about failure. No one wants to tell that story unless there's a happy ending. The fact that you lived out of your car and relied on food stamps is romantic and glorious when told from the perspective of your penthouse apartment, but when you're currently down-at-heel, it's filled with shame. As Alain de Botton famously said, America loves a success story but hates "losers."

While it's nearly impossible to get anyone to discuss their failures in life, and no one wants to ever frame their story as a "loser," I am in the privileged position of interviewing people about their career trajectories for my work and have noticed people often have what I call "career grief," the grief that comes when your career hasn't exactly taken off in the way you would have liked.

Beware of Early Success

Some of the worst examples of career grief are surprisingly from the people who had the most auspicious starts. In the words of Cyril Connolly: Whom the gods wish to destroy, they first call promising. Some of the most heartbreaking stories have come from people who seemed destined for greatness, but for one reason or another, it just didn't quite work out. Joanne* was the recipient of one of the biggest music prizes in the United Kingdom. After being hailed as the next big thing, her career never lived up to its early promise. Fifteen years later, she is now living in a camper van and scraping by on benefits. Occasionally she leafs through a dog-eared scrapbook of press clippings from her first flush of fame. "I really thought I was going to be the biggest recording artist in the world. I know it sounds really big-headed, but my shows were genius. I put so much work into them. It's hard to accept it's not going to happen for me, that that was it." Joanne is still trying to claw her way back to the big time and is currently working on her own self-produced album; "I just can't bring myself to quit, despite everything. It's too heartbreaking. I would literally rather die."

Sunk Cost Fallacy

Why is it so hard to quit, or to use the new buzzword for a career change, to "pivot" to something else? Some people find it incredibly hard to let go of career aspirations, even when they are clearly not yielding results, especially when they have devoted huge portions of their lives to the pursuit. In Joanne's case, 20 years of her life were devoted to her music career, forgoing starting a family and making any financial provisions for her future. In fact, the more time spent on a pursuit, the harder it is to give up, due to a psychological trap called the "sunk cost fallacy." The sunk cost fallacy is when you keep investing time, money, or effort into something just because you've already put so much in, even though it no longer makes sense to continue. You stick with the bad decision to justify the past decision, rather than cutting your losses.

Survivorship Bias

Another reason why people will plough ahead with career ambitions even after they have failed is what's known as survivorship bias. A great example is when we see the likes of Taylor Swift or Lady Gaga imploring people to "never give up on your dreams" as they didn't give up, and look at them now. It's a heartwarming and life-affirming tale, but unfortunately a prime example of survivorship bias. Survivorship bias is when you draw conclusions by looking only at the people or things that made it through some process, while ignoring everyone who didn't. This skews the picture, because you're only seeing the success stories, not the far larger group who tried and failed.

Optimism Bias

The funny thing is, even while knowing the facts and figures about success and failure, people will still try to beat the odds, thinking, well, that's tough for everyone else, but it will work out for me; if I just keep trying, I will be the one to succeed. There's a canny little bit of programming in the human brain which serves us very well in most situations because it allows us to survive in a very scary world; it's called the optimism bias. Optimism bias is the tendency to believe you're less likely than other people to experience bad outcomes, and more likely to succeed, even when the odds are actually the same for everyone. It's why so many people assume they'll be the exception when something has failed for most people who tried it.

The answer to this whole predicament isn't to quit but to realise that whether you succeed or not, it doesn't affect your intrinsic value as a human being. The heartache of "career grief" comes from labelling yourself as a failure. Joanne is still one of the most talented and inspirational female artists you could meet, whether her industry recognises it or not. After many interviews with people suffering from "career grief," I have nothing but empathy for how hard it is to deal with; it's a genuine heartbreak. The grief of unfulfilled career aspirations can be just as devastating as any other form of grief and deserves the same empathy and understanding. In his brilliant book, Status Anxiety, Alain de Botton suggests that this malaise could be alleviated by giving more dignity and respect to what he calls "an ordinary life." I personally have found that a huge part of recovery is self-forgiveness, so much so that I have devoted a whole chapter of my book, How to Get Your Sh*t Together, to it.

In a capitalist society, it can sometimes seem that the only lives of note are the big ones, lit up in lights on a movie theatre, when in reality, every one of us is a unique, lovable, and worthy being, full of potential and intrinsic value, whether we realise it or not.

item.title: Why Story Intelligence Is a New Core Capability
item.description:
Intelligence

Why Story Intelligence Is a New Core Capability

The real human advantage is making better sense of the stories we live by.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • We rarely respond to reality itself. We respond to the stories our minds construct about reality.
  • Story Intelligence is the ability to recognise, question and consciously reshape those stories.
  • As AI produces ever more information, the scarce human skill becomes wise interpretation—not data.
  • Leaders don't just manage people or strategy. They shape the stories through which both are understood.
Story-Intelligence
Source: Steve A. Johnson / Unsplash

Every few decades, a new form of intelligence captures the public imagination. During much of the twentieth century, intelligence was largely equated with IQ. Then came emotional intelligence, reminding us that success depends not only on analytical reasoning, but also on understanding and influencing emotions. More recently, we have become interested in systems thinking, cultural intelligence, interoception and the special gifts of neurodivergent brains.

Another, so far overlooked, form of intelligence deserves a place alongside them: Story Intelligence*. Story intelligence is the ability to recognise, interpret, question and consciously shape the stories that govern our perceptions, emotions and behaviour.

Mistaking Stories for Truth

Most of us underestimate just how profoundly stories shape our lived experience. We tend to think of stories as things we encounter in novels, films or Netflix series. But the most powerful stories are rarely fictional. They are the narratives we continually construct about ourselves, other people and the world.

We rarely experience reality directly. Instead, we experience our interpretation of it. And our interpretations take the forms of stories; we select specific scenes and details and put them into a relation of cause and effect. Because of x, y happened. Because of y, z happened. And so on. Our wellbeing and sense of self are therefore not shaped by reality alone, but to a large extent by the stories we tell ourselves about our reality. These stories are often so familiar that they become invisible. We mistake them for facts or truths.

We may tell ourselves that we are not leadership material, that our bosses do not value us, that we are imposters about to be unmasked and fired, that people cannot be trusted, that we are lacking or defective in numerous ways, or that we are not good enough or fundamentally unlovable. We tell stories about why someone looked at us in a particular way. Why we succeeded or why we failed. Why we belong, or don’t belong.

Many of these stories are simply unhelpful interpretations that have gradually hardened into core beliefs. They are based on a highly selective reading of our lives: a handful of carefully chosen scenes and very specific, often unfair and biased, interpretations of those scenes. Because we dislike cognitive dissonance, we filter new experiences so that they fit with and reinforce the stories we already believe. We are, then, not just storytelling animals, but storytelling animals with serious cognitive blinkers on.

The Evidence Has Been Pointing Towards This for Decades

Psychologists have understood this for a long time. Carl Jung wrote: ‘The most important question anyone can ask is: What myth am I living?’ Narrative psychologists have shown that much of our identity rests on the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves and others. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) distinguishes between helpful and unhelpful interpretations, while Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) distinguishes between thoughts and facts. Both recognise how profoundly our storified interpretations shape our emotions and behaviours. Historians know that societies organise themselves around shared narratives. Organisational psychologists increasingly recognise that workplaces run not only on strategy and incentives, but also on stories.

Story Intelligence brings these insights together into a single, practical, distinctly human capability. It begins with questions many of us rarely pause to ask:

What story am I currently telling myself?

Which experiences and interpretations is this story built on?

Is this story helping me – or holding me back?

What more generative stories might be equally true?

These questions matter because our stories do not merely describe our reality. They actively construct it, shape our emotional and behavioural responses and determine our futures.

Someone who interprets constructive feedback as evidence of rejection will respond very differently from someone who interprets the same conversation as an investment in their development. Two colleagues can experience the same organisational restructuring in radically different ways. One sees opportunity. The other sees threat and betrayal. The external reality may be identical. The stories are not.

Why Story Intelligence Matters

Story intelligence matters more than ever because we are entering an era of extraordinary technological capability combined with unprecedented interpretive uncertainty.

Artificial intelligence can generate reports, answer questions, analyse enormous datasets and produce persuasive information in seconds. However, it cannot determine what that information means for us and which parts of it are truly relevant. Meaning- and sense-making remain profoundly human capabilities.

AI may tell us that our industry is changing. It cannot tell us whether to interpret that change as catastrophe, liberation or opportunity for reinvention. It can summarise a medical diagnosis. It cannot determine the story we construct about living with illness. It can analyse economic forecasts. It cannot decide whether uncertainty is a reason to withdraw our investments in fear or to experiment more courageously. Our decision depends on the stories we tell about the facts.

Indeed, the more information AI generates, the greater the premium on wise and discerning human interpretation and story awareness becomes. The scarce resource is no longer information itself. It is the ability to make good sense of and tell generative stories about it.

Organisations Live Inside Stories, Too

Story intelligence therefore matters not only for personal wellbeing, but also for leadership, organisational life and society more broadly.

Organisations, too, live inside stories. Strategies succeed or fail not simply because they are analytically sound, but because employees construct stories about what those strategies mean for them. Leaders who understand these hidden narratives gain access to one of the most powerful – and overlooked – drivers of organisational behaviour.

One of the most common assumptions I encounter in my work with organisations is that people resist change. I am not convinced this is usually true. More often, people resist the meaning they attach to change: A restructuring becomes a story about the threat of redundancy and uncertainty, and about leadership incompetency. Artificial intelligence becomes a story about human obsolescence. Change becomes a story about loss and energy-wastage. The strategic plan itself is rarely the problem. The stories people construct around it often are.

Becoming the Author Rather Than the Prisoner

The same principle applies in our private lives. A difficult conversation becomes a story about rejection. Failure becomes a story about identity rather than behaviour or learning. Exhaustion becomes a story about personal inadequacy instead of a signal that something structural or behavioural requires our attention.

The stories we live inside determine what we notice, what we remember, how we feel and what we believe is possible.

The good news is that our stories are not written in stone. Story intelligence is not about replacing every difficult thought with a positive one. Nor is it about pretending painful realities do not exist; some stories are true and need to be heard and acted on. Instead, it is about becoming aware that our minds are continually interpreting experience – and recognising that interpretation is often far more flexible than we assume.

The most story-intelligent people I know share one quality above all others: they hold their own narratives lightly. They remain curious about the stories they are telling themselves and are also curious about other people's stories. They notice when an interpretation is masquerading as a fact. They are willing to revise their narratives when new evidence emerges. They become active authors rather than passive prisoners of their stories.

item.title: A Healing Meditation Using Internal Family Systems
item.description:
Meditation

A Healing Meditation Using Internal Family Systems

Self-care to unburden stress and anxiety and create pathways toward healing.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Setting aside just 10-15 minutes a day for meditation can change your life.
  • Internal Family Systems approaches encourage you to look inside at all your “parts” and reflect.
  • An IFS-style meditation can help unburden stress and anxiety and create pathways toward healing.

If you’re like me, your day-to-day is full of endless tasks and a multitude of pressures and demands. How could I possibly find the time for self-care and, much less, meditation? And even if I had time, where would I start?

Setting aside just 10-15 minutes a day for meditation can change your life. Here I provide my favorite healing meditation using Internal Family Systems (IFS) to help unburden stress and anxiety and create pathways toward healing.

Source: Cup of Couple / Pexels

Internal Family Systems

The IFS model of therapeutic practice has become wildly popular (e.g., Schwartz, 2021). The approach encourages you to look inside at all your “parts,” reflect on what they are telling you, and work to unburden past harm and trauma. Instead of trying to change ourselves, IFS acknowledges “All parts are welcome.” IFS helps us heal from the inside out—just like the Disney Pixar movie series title (which is loosely based on IFS!). By getting to know our parts, we can also locate our truest sense of Self (capital “S”).

The founder of IFS, Richard C. Schwartz, outlines the four basic goals of IFS in his book, No Bad Parts (2021). They are:

  1. Liberate parts from the roles they’ve been forced into, so they can be who they’re designed to be.
  2. Restore trust in the Self and self-leadership.
  3. Reharmonize the inner system.
  4. Become more Self-led in your interactions with the world.

In my own self-care work with IFS, I have practiced many different meditations. Merging such practices with my own goals, I have come up with my favorite one. I hope you will try it out!

Source: Katrin Bolovtsova / Pexels

Daily Meditation: Hello Parts! Hello Self!

This is a short and restorative meditation that you can do every day. It is a check-in with your part(s) and a way to connect with your true Self. It is partially adapted from Schwartz’s exercise “Unblending and Embodying” (2021).

  • Start by getting relaxed and comfortable. Maybe sit in your favorite chair or even lie on the ground. Try to minimize any noise around you or play soothing sounds and/or music. Close your eyes and take a few deep cleansing breaths.
  • Now let your parts speak to you. Which part is talking loudest? What is it saying? If nobody is talking, invite them to speak up, but make them feel comfortable by telling them you are here to listen to what they are concerned about. If too many parts are talking, invite one to the forefront and tell the others you promise to check in with them soon.
  • After identifying a one-on-one interaction with the loudest part, create an open space for you both to take the time to chat. It might help to visualize the part as a color, object, or even a figure. It might sound silly, but it really helps me to talk to something I can visualize. Some talking points you might have with your part might be: What is going on today? How are you feeling? What are you most concerned about? Then wait and listen.
  • After the part responds to your questions, reassure your part that you are here to help. Tell the part they don’t have to struggle alone. Remind them that you have the strength to work together to figure this out and heal.
  • With the conversation going, let your part share its fears and concerns. Acknowledge and validate those feelings. If you’re new to IFS, you might need to remind your part that it probably doesn’t know you very well yet and tell your part you hope to get better acquainted. Though it may seem odd to want to get to know a part that is stressing you out, IFS reminds us that knowing our parts is necessary in order to unburden them, make them feel safe and cozy, and work toward healing.
  • If you are able, tell the part it can relax. Maybe even visualize the part getting comfy. Explain that you are a competent adult who is able to handle the situation at hand (because many parts are stuck or lingering in our childhood selves).
  • Here is the segment I enjoy most: With that open space of relaxation, you might notice a sense of harmony taking over your body. If you don’t notice this immediately, take a few more deep breaths. Sometimes you might even feel your body shifting toward an overwhelming sense of restful calmness. But if you don’t, not to worry! You might need to get to know this part more deeply before you experience this type of release.
  • If your part is comfy enough to separate, what IFS calls “unblending,” your true sense of Self-energy might show up and hang out a bit. Self-energy feels different for everyone, but many describe it as a humming sense that creates an overall feeling of equanimity, or Zen. For me, it is fun to visualize self-energy as a ball of light, glitter, or shining waves of sun. Take a few breaths and sit inside the feelings you are having with Self-energy. Sometimes I even hear soothing sounds such as crashing waves, so remember to check in with all five senses during this process. This helps with recognizing how the embodiment of Self feels to you.
  • When you are ready, thank your part for coming out to chat. Remind it that you know it is important. Reassure it that you will be back soon to check in with it and that it can trust you (similar to what you might tell an anxious child to help them feel safe and supported). You might even give your sense of Self a hug too.
  • Now gradually open your eyes, take a few more deep breaths, and come back into the world—recharged and ready for what is next.
Source: Lukas Rychvalsky / Pexels

I hope you enjoyed this meditation and spending time with your Self. This practice serves as a reminder that “Like the sun, the Self can be temporarily obscured, but it never disappears” (Schwartz, 2021).

item.title: The Art of the Apology
item.description:
Forgiveness

The Art of the Apology

Most apologoes fall flat. They don't have to.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Many apologies fail because they omit components the injured person needs to hear
  • Research shows accepting responsibility is the single most important element of an effective apology.
  • Forgiveness belongs to the person you hurt. An apology that demands it becomes a transaction.

"I'm sorry you feel that way."

"Mistakes were made."

"I apologize, but..."

We have all received apologies like these—and felt worse afterward. Words of contrition were technically present, yet something essential was missing. The apology was not taken seriously, or it was judged insufficient, and the relationship stayed bruised.

Research on conflict repair shows that apologies vary enormously in effectiveness, and that most of that variation comes down to structure: which components an apology contains, not how emotional it sounds. In a series of studies, Lewicki and colleagues (2016) tested six candidate components and found that apologies became dramatically more effective as more components were included—and that some components mattered far more than others.

Apologizing well is hard for a reason. Admitting fault threatens our self-image as good, competent people, which is precisely why we reach for hedges, justifications, and passive voice (Schumann, 2018). An effective apology requires overriding that self-protective reflex. These are the five steps research suggests that a complete apology should contain:

Step 1: Acknowledge the Pain

Before anything else, name the harm. The person you hurt needs to hear that you see their loss or pain—specifically, not generically. "I know my comment embarrassed you in front of the team" may be welcome; "I'm sorry for whatever upset you" will not be.

This step matters because an injured person's first question is not "Are you sorry?" but "Do you understand what you did?" Perceived understanding of the offense is a strong predictor of whether victims judge an apology sincere. Skipping it—or blurring it—signals that you either don't grasp the harm or don't consider it real.

Step 2: Own That You Caused It

After acknowledging pain, one must acknowledge responsibility. "I'm sorry you were hurt" locates the event in the other person's feelings; "I'm sorry I hurt you" locates it in your actions.

In Lewicki and colleagues' (2016) component studies, acknowledgment of responsibility emerged as the single most important element of an effective apology. It is also the one people most reliably dodge—through passive constructions ("mistakes were made"), conditional phrasing ("if anyone was offended"), or the small word that undoes everything: "but." The moment a justification follows the apology, listeners reclassify it as a defense (Schumann, 2014).

Step 3: Express Genuine Remorse—Without Justification

Now, and only now, say you are sorry—and let the sentence end. Expressions of regret work when they follow acknowledgment of harm and responsibility; offered alone, they read as social lubricant rather than repentance.

Genuine remorse also means resisting the urge to explain why the offense was understandable. Explanations of what happened can help; excuses for it cannot. Research on defensive responding shows that transgressors who feel their self-worth is threatened produce more justifications and less complete apologies—and that shoring up one's sense of self first produces notably less defensive, higher-quality apologies (Schumann, 2014). If you feel the "but" rising, that is the signal to pause, not to speak.

Step 4: Offer Repair

Words acknowledge the past; repair addresses it. Ask—or better, propose—what you can do to make it right, Whether it's correcting the record with the people who witnessed the insult, replacing what was damaged, or redoing the work, make the time.

In the component research, offer of repair ranked second in importance after responsibility (Lewicki et al., 2016). And a broad meta-analysis of forgiveness research finds that conciliatory gestures—apology paired with compensation or amends—reliably predict victims' willingness to forgive (Fehr, Gelfand, & Nag, 2010). Repair converts an apology from a statement into an act. Even when full restoration is impossible, the offer itself communicates that you take the cost seriously.

Step 5: Commit to Change

Finally, address the future: what will be different so this does not happen again. Not a vague "I'll do better," but something checkable—"I will ask before sharing anything you tell me privately."

This step answers the injured person's forward-looking question: "Am I safe with you now?" Declarations of repentance signal that the offense reflected a lapse you intend to correct, not a pattern you intend to continue. An apology without changed behavior is, over time, simply a request to be excused repeatedly.

What Not to Do

The five steps also clarify why familiar formulas fail. "I'm sorry you feel that way" performs Step 3 while explicitly ignoring Steps 1 and 2. "Mistakes were made" gestures at Step 2 while deleting the actor. "I apologize, but you have to understand..." completes Step 3 and then retracts it. Each is experienced not as a partial apology but as a counterfeit one—which is often worse than silence, because it adds condescension to the original injury.

One more caution: Do not demand forgiveness as the price of your apology. Forgiveness is the injured person's to give, on their timeline. An apology that ends with "...so are we good now?" converts a gift into a transaction.

Notice the architecture: the sequence moves from their experience (Step 1), to your role (Step 2), to your feeling (Step 3), to your action (Step 4), and to your future (Step 5). Most failed apologies run this order in reverse—leading with the apologizer's feelings and intentions and never quite arriving at the other person's pain.

A complete apology is uncomfortable. It is supposed to be; the discomfort is the cost of the repair, and the person you hurt can tell whether you paid it. But the research is encouraging on one point: apologizing well follows a structure that anyone can learn, practice, and, when it matters most, deliver.

item.title: Do Winners Really Never Quit?
item.description:
Motivation

Do Winners Really Never Quit?

Knowing when to say "when" can be just as important as pushing through.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Persistence matters. So does knowing when a goal no longer serves you.
  • The healthiest choice isn't always pushing forward. Sometimes it's pausing and redirecting.
  • Recovery isn't the opposite of progress. It's part of progress.

Lately, I've been thinking a lot about quitting. Specifically, whether I should quit my marathon training just one month before race day. Before you remind me how close I am, how much work I've put in, or tell me I'll regret it forever, hear me out.

It’s got me thinking about what the science says about quitting.

For most of my life, I've subscribed to a "never quit" philosophy. It's served me well, personally and professionally. I've completed five marathons, a dissertation, and a book, so I know the satisfaction that comes from putting in the work, trusting the process, and crossing the literal or figurative finish line.

But this time feels different.

This isn't about motivation or whether I can do hard things. It's about competing life demands and a growing sense that my body isn't recovering the way it should. Running has always been my therapy. During this training cycle, there have been days when getting out the door and putting miles under my feet was exactly what I needed to clear my head. That's what makes this decision so difficult. Running has been both part of the solution and, increasingly, I fear, part of the strain.

For some of us, the harder challenge isn't learning how to persevere.

It's learning when not to.

We celebrate grit. We tell ourselves that winners never quit. And there’s a great deal of science to support the benefits of perseverance and grit. Pushing through discomfort in pursuit of one’s goals can make you stronger and more resilient. I've experienced that firsthand, both in marathons and in life.

But science tells us there is also a flip side to that coin.

Sometimes healthy self-regulation isn't just about persistence or positive thinking. It's also about recognizing when a goal no longer serves us and redirecting our energy toward goals that do. Across multiple studies, people who are better able to disengage from unattainable goals and reengage with new ones report better psychological well-being, lower distress, and even better physical health compared to people who persist at all costs.

That doesn't mean quitting whenever something gets hard. Far from it.

It means asking a different question. Not only, Can I keep going? But rather, Should I? Is this goal still serving me? That is the key question.

As someone who studies sleep, I'm reminded that recovery isn't the opposite of progress. It's where progress happens. The same may be true of our goals. If we relentlessly pursue goals that no longer serve us, we may miss the opportunity to invest in the ones that matter most.

Maybe a better way to think of this is not “quitting.” It’s letting go.

I'm still not sure what I'll do. I'll decide after my next long run.

item.title: When the Tool Becomes the Threat
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

When the Tool Becomes the Threat

Every generation decides which help counts as cheating. The list keeps changing.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • The typewriter had resistance. You had to mean it. Then it got easier.
  • I write with a pen, a stylus, my voice, and sometimes a machine that cleans it up.
  • Someone changed the speed limit and added a zero at the end.
  • The question came from 46 years of listening, not from any machine.

I remember the typewriter in my father's office. The keys were hard to push all the way down. The letters wore away on what I thought was marble but was probably just plastic. There was a click to it. A resistance. You had to mean it.

Then the electric typewriter arrived and everything got smoother. Easier. Something like the difference between a stick shift and an automatic, or a bicycle and a motorcycle. Things were gained. Things were also lost. We just did not always know which was which until later.

I have been thinking about that lately because I am writing again and the question of how to write has become more complicated than it used to be.

I love to write. I am also hesitant to write. I go back and forth between a pen, which feels more soulful to me, and my digital notepad that requires a stylus but no real ink. Is that still writing with a pen? I am not sure. I also dictate sometimes, speak my draft out loud and have it transcribed. Sometimes I ask a tool to clean it up, catch the grammatical errors I tend to make, help it sound a little more like me than the raw draft does. And then I wonder. Is that mine? Is that legitimate? Is it honest? Is it genuine? Is it aligned? Can I stand by it?

These are not small questions. And yet the world keeps moving faster. Someone changed the speed limit and added a zero at the end. What used to feel like 70 miles per hour is now 700. You cannot get through it competently without the tools that are available. I use them. I get away with it. The people on the other end feel heard. A machine assisted at some very real level.

I remember when earbuds first appeared. I was one of the first people to wear one, that little flashing thing in my ear, talking to nobody visible. People were bothered by it. Scared maybe. Offended. Now nearly everyone has something in their ears and nobody thinks twice.

I wonder if we are in that same moment now with the tools that think alongside us. Not quite there yet. Still in the part where people are bothered. Still in the part where the flashing light in the ear feels like a threat to something they cannot quite name.

What I keep returning to is this. The tool did not write the question I am sitting with. The question came from somewhere older and quieter than any machine I have ever used. It came from 46 years of listening to people try to say what is true about themselves and wondering whether they were being heard.

At what point does the tool become the threat? And at what point does our resistance to the tool become the real problem?

item.title: When Forgetfulness Is Not Just Aging
item.description:
ADHD

When Forgetfulness Is Not Just Aging

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in older adults.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • ADHD in later life is frequently mistaken for normal aging, depression, or early-stage dementia.
  • Greater awareness can improve diagnosis and treatment in this growing population.
  • Later-age diagnosis can be transformative, improving quality of life and overall well-being.

By Aakanksha Singh, MD, and Narpinder K. Malhi, MD, members of the Committee on Family at the Group for the Advancement of Psychiatry

When a young adult struggles with inattention, difficulty managing tasks, and trouble completing responsibilities, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is often one of the first diagnoses that comes to mind.

However, what happens when these same challenges appear in an older adult, someone who is forgetful, disorganized, and has difficulty recalling names? Should it be thought of as ADHD, or should it be assumed it is simply a part of aging?

Eleanor, a 72-year-old retired teacher, had always been organized and dependable, but had to put in extra effort and work long hours to maintain this level of functioning. In recent years, however, she began misplacing items, missing appointments, and struggling with routine tasks.

At first, she attributed these changes to aging, but her daughter encouraged her to seek help. Despite two prior evaluations for memory concerns, both with normal results, her difficulties persisted. A more comprehensive assessment revealed a different explanation: ADHD, a diagnosis she had never imagined having at her age.

Eleanor’s story raises an important question: When older adults experience forgetfulness and disorganization, these symptoms might reflect more than normal aging—perhaps a lifelong condition that has gone unnoticed?

Diagnosing ADHD

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by patterns of inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. Although often associated with onset in childhood, ADHD can persist across the lifespan. Increasing recognition of ADHD in the general population likely reflects a combination of improved health literacy, greater public awareness through media and social platforms, and changes in diagnostic practices.

Research estimates that approximately 2.18 percent of older adults meet criteria for ADHD, highlighting a growing need for clinical awareness and appropriate care. Emerging evidence also suggests that ADHD may be more common in older adults than previously thought, although it remains underdiagnosed in this population.

Despite this increasing recognition, identifying ADHD in older adults is a challenge. Many of the diagnosis’ core features present differently with age and can overlap with typical cognitive changes. For example, instead of overt hyperactivity, symptoms often appear as difficulties with executive functioning, the latter being a term referring to the mental skills used to plan, organize, manage time, and complete tasks. These challenges may appear as forgetfulness, trouble following instructions, or difficulty keeping track of daily responsibilities.

For individuals like Eleanor, these symptoms can be misattributed to normal aging or early cognitive impairment. Even after extensive testing, persistent inattention may continue to be interpreted primarily as a memory problem rather than part of a broader pattern of ADHD. This misattribution can delay appropriate diagnosis and treatment, affecting a person’s quality of life and day-to-day functioning.

The Hidden Burden of ADHD in Older Adults

ADHD in older adults rarely exists in isolation. It is often accompanied by a range of other mental health conditions that can complicate making a diagnosis and contribute to overall impairment. Substance use, including alcohol, nicotine, and other drugs, is frequently reported in individuals with ADHD.

Psychological well-being is also affected. Lower self-esteem, reduced confidence, and diminished quality of life are frequently reported, often shaped by years of unrecognized and untreated symptoms. Social and interpersonal relationships may be similarly affected. Individuals with ADHD often describe feeling misunderstood, socially isolated, or in conflict with others, sometimes leading to smaller support networks and greater emotional loneliness.

Despite these challenges, individuals with ADHD often possess unique strengths and abilities. Many individuals describe creativity, enthusiasm, and the ability to focus intensely on topics of interest as positive traits. Over time, adaptive coping strategies may emerge, contributing to resilience and continued engagement in meaningful activities in later life.

How Can Mental Health Professionals Help?

Things mental health professionals can do to support older individuals with concerns for ADHD include:

  • Prior to making a diagnosis of ADHD, clinicians should consider other conditions such as mild cognitive impairment, anxiety, substance-related factors, and behavioral factors. Clinicians should also inquire about the onset and persistence of symptoms as well as obtain a detailed developmental and family history.
  • Perform a comprehensive medical workup to rule out other causes, such as thyroid dysfunction and seizure disorders, before establishing the diagnosis.
  • Medications such as stimulants and nonstimulants can be considered after careful evaluation of cardiovascular health and potential drug interactions.
  • Psychotherapeutic interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), when adapted for ADHD, can help individuals develop organizational strategies and improve emotional regulation while also addressing longstanding patterns of self-doubt that may accompany years of unrecognized symptoms.
  • ADHD coaching may provide additional practical support, focusing on skills such as time management, prioritization, and task completion.
  • Environmental and lifestyle modifications, including structured routines, regular physical activity, and the use of reminders or simplified schedules, can further enhance daily functioning

Once she had a diagnosis in place, Eleanor began treatment with Vyvanse 20 mg, and she gradually noticed improvement. She became more organized, kept track of appointments, and felt less overwhelmed. More importantly, knowing the diagnosis helped her make sense of lifelong challenges she had once blamed on herself. For Eleanor, understanding her condition brought clarity and a renewed sense of control, highlighting that even later in life, recognizing ADHD can lead to meaningful change.

item.title: Ghost Thought—A Ghostwriter for the Mind, Not the Page
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Ghost Thought—A Ghostwriter for the Mind, Not the Page

What happens when we surrender the thought before we've even had it?

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Ghostwriting borrowed your words, AI is borrowing the thought before it forms.
  • A "ghost thought" arrives dressed as your own, with nothing lost to remember.
  • Skipping the clumsy first draft of a thought costs more than we realize.
Source: Joshua Woroniecki / Pixabay

Ghostwriting has always had a clear division of labor. Someone else does the writing. You supply the thinking and the life it's drawn from. The words are borrowed. The mind behind them is not.

Emergence of "Ghost Thought"

But today, I've been noticing something like the reverse. Call it a ghost thought. It's a thought you never quite had, that arrives already dressed in your own words. The thinking gets farmed out. The writing, oddly, is almost never the problem, as it shows up with the validation and approval of technology's new step in innovation and convenience. What's missing isn't the sentence. It's whatever used to happen before the sentence.

That's the part I find both curious and strange. We built an enormous amount of anxiety around artificial intelligence (AI) and writing, as if the words were the valuable part. But the words were always the easy half, and ghostwriters proved that decades ago for politicians and executives and anyone with a story. The words were never sacred. The thinking was supposed to be the part that stayed uniquely yours.

But let's take a step back. There's a moment before you open that chat window when something is already happening. A thought has started to assemble itself, not fully, just enough that it can take a more complete shape, if you waited. Most days you don't wait. You type before it finishes, and something else finishes it for you. AI doesn't just answer the question; it answers before your own thinking has taken any shape at all. And then it hands you back prose good enough that you never notice the void where your own answer would have been.

None of this matters much as a single event. But string enough of them together, across small and varied decisions that used to be yours to contemplate, and it stops looking like convenience. It starts looking like a habit of arriving places you've never been to.

Why Struggling With Ideas Matters

A lot of good ideas don't show up as complete thoughts or answers. Frequently, they show up clumsy and half-baked, perhaps even a bit annoying. And that discomfort has a rather critical purpose. AI is remarkably good at skipping straight past the struggle right to the fluent response. The price isn't just that we think less; it's that we stop finding out what the clumsy version might have become. And it's that cognitive path from A to B where we find the toil, the imagination, and even the aha moment. You see, when the mind stumbles, it grows. AI doesn't give you a cushion to fall on; it often eliminates the entire journey.

Ghostwriting always made the trade rather explicit, almost as a functional Faustian bargain. You knew whose words those were, even if the world didn't. You also paid a price. Ghost thought doesn't announce itself in a similar fashion. It hands the writing back so perfectly that you mistake it for arrival, when what you actually got arrives as a counterfeit of you. And that may be a price too high to pay.

item.title: The Cost of Misdiagnosing Postpartum Psychosis
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

The Cost of Misdiagnosing Postpartum Psychosis

Being heard can mean the difference between two very different outcomes.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Postpartum psychosis affects one to two per 1,000 births and is a serious psychiatric emergency.
  • Standard postpartum care is typically one six-week visit, which leaves a significant gap in care.
  • Being dismissed by providers can have dire consequences, but being heard and believed can save lives.

Postpartum psychosis is a serious mental health condition that can have devastating consequences if left untreated. Right now, this reality is being played out in a Massachusetts courtroom, where Lindsay Clancy stands trial for the deaths of her three children. Her case has reignited a difficult but important conversation about what can happen when the mental health system fails a mother in crisis.

Unfortunately, Clancy is not the only mother failed by the system. Postpartum psychosis awareness advocate Aaisha Alvi, author of the memoir A Mom Like That, knows this all too well. She survived her own experience with postpartum psychosis after being dismissed by several providers. Both her and Clancy’s stories point to the same urgent gaps in perinatal mental health care.

What Is Postpartum Psychosis?

Postpartum psychosis is a serious psychiatric condition that occurs in an estimated one to two out of every 1,000 births. It typically develops rapidly, often within the first few weeks after birth, but it can occur later. It’s important to note that women who have experienced pregnancy loss can also develop postpartum psychosis.

The hallmark of postpartum psychosis is a break with reality, which can involve hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not actually there), delusions (false beliefs that the person is convinced are true), and severely disorganized thinking. Women with postpartum psychosis require emergency psychiatric treatment because of the risk of suicide and infanticide if left untreated. In the case of postpartum psychosis, delaying treatment can be fatal.

Despite the fact that postpartum psychosis is recognized by perinatal providers as a severe mental health condition, it is not currently recognized as a standalone diagnosis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), the manual professionals use to diagnose mental health conditions. This makes it harder for healthcare providers to identify its symptoms consistently and contributes to a lack of provider education on warning signs, as well as stigma.

Why Dismissal and Misdiagnosis Happen

There are several factors that contribute to providers missing or misdiagnosing postpartum psychosis. In some cases, the early stages of postpartum psychosis can look like postpartum depression or anxiety. Mothers who do speak up might be told that what they are experiencing is “just the baby blues” or “normal new mom worries.” They might be assured that they’ll feel better soon and to wait it out, or provided with a referral for therapy or medication with no follow-up.

Many healthcare providers are not formally trained in identifying and treating postpartum psychosis. When the diagnosis is unclear, providers may try different types of medications that may worsen symptoms.

Additionally, postpartum follow-up care in the United States is typically limited to one six-week visit. Because of how rapidly postpartum psychosis can develop and escalate, this limited window of time lowers the chances of catching it early.

Lindsay Clancy's Case

Lindsay Clancy is a former labor and delivery nurse from Boston currently facing trial for the deaths of her three children in January 2023. Clancy had voluntarily sought treatment multiple times in the months leading up to the tragedy. She was also prescribed several different medications.

Clancy’s defense team argues that she was suffering from untreated postpartum psychosis and that the treatment she did receive failed to address her condition. Her case has brought national attention to our nation’s fragmented mental health care system, and the inconsistent ways that postpartum psychiatric emergencies are addressed.

Aaisha Alvi's Story

Aaisha Alvi herself has lived experience of postpartum psychosis and is an advocate who has shared her story in her memoir. In A Mom Like That, Alvi details how she experienced command hallucinations and delusions to hurt her daughter. Like Clancy, she shared what was happening with multiple providers and was dismissed every time. Fortunately, she eventually did meet with a doctor who accurately identified that what she was experiencing was postpartum psychosis and took action.

Alvi has reflected that the difference between her outcome and Clancy’s came down to being properly listened to. If she hadn’t found a provider that took her symptoms seriously, her story could have ended differently. Since then, her advocacy work has been aimed at making sure that other mothers don’t fall through the cracks.

What Needs to Change

Stories like these reveal the serious gaps in how perinatal mental health concerns are addressed. This is especially noteworthy for women of color, who are both more likely to experience perinatal mental health concerns and less likely to receive treatment for them, as Alvi also points out in her book.

Postpartum follow-up care needs to go beyond one visit in six weeks, especially for mothers at risk of mental health concerns. And providers who work with perinatal women need to be trained in postpartum psychosis. Most importantly, new mothers need to be taken seriously when they say something is wrong.

If you or someone you know is showing signs of postpartum psychosis, such as rapid changes in mental state, hallucinations, or delusions, you need to take action right away. Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. Contact a healthcare provider or go to your nearest emergency room. Do not wait for these symptoms to get better on their own.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Surprising Benefits of Being Alone
item.description:
Loneliness

The Surprising Benefits of Being Alone

Why solitude may be one of the most overlooked relationship skills.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Being alone and feeling lonely are not the same thing.
  • The ability to be alone can be considered a relationship skill—not a sign of isolation.
  • Solitude may be one way to strengthen your own internal nurturing presence.
Source: GoodInteractive / Pixabay

As a therapist, I’ve noticed that people often feel afraid of being alone—yes, that includes going on a walk or to dinner alone or spending the weekend alone. They’ll sometimes spend time with activities or people that don’t add to their lives just to avoid it.

A few common explanations come up repeatedly. Some feel uncomfortable being seen alone. They don't want people judging them or making assumptions about why they're, for example, at the movies alone. Others feel uncomfortable not having someone to share their in-the-moment thoughts with. Still others worry about the anxiety they feel while alone or the vulnerability of it: Will someone invade my space? Will I have to be mean to shut it down? What if no one wants to connect—then what does that mean about me?

Many have conscious and unconscious meanings they’ve attached to being alone that may be limiting. Yet, there can be surprising benefits—even superpowers—that come from solitude, and being alone is quite different from feeling lonely. That distinction matters because many people avoid being alone in an effort to avoid loneliness—that sense of yearning for connection.

Being Alone vs. Being Lonely

Being alone is a physical state. Being lonely is an emotional experience. They are not the same. Being alone can benefit a person—it creates space to be with yourself rather than consciously and unconsciously orienting around others.

Donald Winnicott’s "The Capacity to Be Alone" beautifully defines and reflects this idea. The ability to be comfortably alone reflects emotional maturity. This capacity can support clearer career focus, stronger mental health, and more grounded partnerships.

Potential Benefits of Solitude

Being alone can:

  • allow you to turn toward what matters to you, without the pull to accommodate others.
  • create space for uninterrupted thought, where possibilities can form and expand.
  • deepen awareness, which can support understanding others and increased empathy.
  • help you meet the many, multidimensional parts of yourself so that you can come from a calm space, even when life gets heated.

In uninterrupted space, you can focus on your core values and the accompanying boundaries, which can set you up for more ongoing satisfaction in life.

Being Alone Is Often Learned From Being Alone in Another’s Presence

Winnicott’s article points out something powerful about how we learn to be alone—it’s often from being alone in the presence of another. Their emotional support gradually becomes an internal sense of safety that no longer requires another person's physical presence. Think of a calm caregiver being present with a crying baby until the baby’s nervous system settles.

If we never give ourselves opportunities to be alone, we may never discover that we can become a source of steadiness for ourselves. Instead, we may keep reaching for whoever is available, whether or not those relationships actually help us feel safe.

Relationships can pull us away from knowing ourselves—especially when we become focused on pleasing others. It is often in solitude (being alone) that we can meet and accept the parts of ourselves we have otherwise been able to avoid. From that kind of intimacy, "possibility" can emerge.

Solitude is not the opposite of a relationship. Instead, it can strengthen our ability for healthy relationships with self and others.

How to Be OK With Being Alone More Often

For those not used to being alone, the "bravery" might start small. It can look like staying with yourself for a few extra minutes before reaching for distraction or choosing a brief solo activity (e.g., a walk to the corner close by), and noticing what comes up.

The goal is not to feel comfortable right away; it’s to build familiarity with yourself—over time. Sometimes the relationship we neglect most is the one that actually matters most: our relationship with ourselves.

Solitude may be one way to strengthen your own internal nurturing presence. In our busy world, solitude may be needed to keep meeting more of yourself—and accepting those parts with compassion and curiosity instead of anxiety or judgment.

For those interested in self-development (and I assume that is you since you are reading this), the ability to be alone might even be considered a vital relationship skill.

item.title: Random Error: Implications for Consciousness Research
item.description:
Consciousness

Random Error: Implications for Consciousness Research

Understanding random error is critical for studying the machinery of the mind.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Researchers distinguish two kinds of noise in psychology experiments: "systematic error" vs. "random error."
  • To make progress in the study of consciousness, it is important to appreciate the nature of random error.
  • Random error usually cannot undermine the validity of a properly designed experiment.

When designing experiments, one is on the lookout for confounds. These are systematic, consistent differences between the experimental and the control conditions, differences that the experimenter is unaware of. They undermine validity. The only difference between the conditions should be the variable of interest.

Systematic vs. Random Errors

Imagine that caffeine is your variable of interest. You're interested in the effects of caffeine on reaction time to a beep. The experimental condition might have participants drink caffeinated coffee, and the control condition, with a different group of participants, might have them drink decaf. Apart from the presence of caffeine, everything else between the conditions should be the same, including the roast and temperature of the coffee. If, by accident, the temperature of the coffee was always higher in one condition than the other, then this would be a potential confound. Any effect of the temperature would be an unwanted effect; hence, it is called noise or “error.” Because the difference in temperature is constant between the conditions, this kind of error is known as “systematic error.” Thus, confounds are a kind of systematic error.

Then there is noise (or error) that experiments try to minimize but that is not systematic. These are variables that differ across participants but that do not differ systematically between the conditions. With a sufficient sample size per condition, these random effects should “wash out.” For example, it might be that Participant 2 in the caffeinated condition worked a night shift and was tired and so had slow reaction times. Or it could be that Participant 6 in the decaffeinated condition is an expert video gamer and always has fast reaction times. Maybe Participant 30 in the caffeinated condition did not understand the instructions of the task and thought that he or she should respond as slowly as possible and not as quickly as possible. All of these sources of noise are known as “random error” and, in a properly designed study, should not lead to invalid effects. Only systematic, consistent differences between the two conditions can lead to invalid effects (“systematic error”). Experimenters try to minimize the sources of random error as much as possible. By having a sufficiently large sample size, such effects should be negligible and not lead to a consequential difference in the effect between the experimental and control conditions.

Enter consciousness research. In many types of research in the field of consciousness, the experimenter presents the experimental participant with a stimulus and then records the participant's conscious experience. The stimulus could be a visual object or a visual stimulus that causes an illusion.

Source: SHOX ART / Pexels

Let’s take a simple case. The participant is instructed to look at the center of a computer screen and report what visual stimulus is presented on the screen momentarily (one second). Thus, a red apple is presented briefly on the screen. Most participants will report seeing a red apple. Thus, “red apple” would be the most common response. As a matter of fact, most research indicates that participants cannot help but activate the percept and even the meaning of a stimulus when it is presented in this way. Newer research reveals that such a stimulus can automatically activate even autobiographical memories associated with the stimulus. For example, one participant might perceive the stimulus and then activate the memory, perhaps unconsciously, of years ago giving an apple to an elementary school teacher.

But not all participants will report “red apple.” Some might have accidentally looked away from the screen during that one second in which the stimulus was presented, because, for example, they had to cough. Maybe some participants closed their eyes while the stimulus was presented. Maybe some have red-green color blindness and could not tell whether the apple was a red apple or a green apple. These participants might have reported just “an apple.” Perhaps one of the participants was a green grocer and reported “McIntosh,” which is the name of a particular kind of apple. One could think of many other cases in which the experience and response of the participant might not be “red apple.” These would all be cases of random error. For this particular experiment, the random error is not informative.

If the result was that 90 percent of the participants reported “red apple,” it would not mean that the apple stimulus does not normally activate the same response in the remaining 10 percent of the participants. Again, the stimulus might not have had that effect only because, for example, the participant happened to look away from the screen. The 10 percent of trials in which participants did not report “red apple” could consist of a medley of kinds of random error.

Implications for Research on Consciousness

These considerations have implications for research on consciousness. People often think of conscious thoughts as whimsical and difficult to predict. Research has shown that conscious thoughts in response to a stimulus are predictable to a substantive extent. With these considerations in mind, one could argue that, when presenting a participant with a red apple or some other visual stimulus, or, to make it more interesting, when presenting a participant with a particular visual illusion, the private conscious response in the typical participant will be this or that, a prediction based on prior observations or theory. Because the inter-individual differences across participants are treated as random error, knowledge of what a stimulus evokes (on average) is knowledge of the effects of the stimulus on the conscious mind.

From this standpoint, knowing what a stimulus evokes in consciousness (with some degree of certainty) is the same as knowing what a person will experience in response to that stimulus. Let me provide a more concrete example. I will present you with two words. Your task is not to think of a word associated with these two words. The two words will be written in uppercase. Again, your task is not to think of an associate of these two words. Here are the two words: LEASH WALK. Any thoughts come to mind? Most people will think “dog.” This is the effect of this stimulus. Knowledge of the effect of this stimulus is knowledge of how the consciousnesses of, say, Peter, Sussie, and Bob will react to the stimulus, as private and as whimsical as their consciousnesses might be. Now, it might be that, when presented with those two words, Ted, another participant, thought “Fido,” because that was the name of his dog. This idiosyncratic effect would be a case of random error. It would not be evidence against how knowledge is activated in the conscious mind by external stimuli.
