item.title: Mall World: Are People Dreaming of the Same Place?
item.description:
Dreaming

Mall World: Are People Dreaming of the Same Place?

A guide to understanding locations in your dreams.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Locations in dreams ground the dream experience.
  • The details of location provide a sense- and memory-based reference point.
  • The locating aspect of dreams is a lens for understanding a specific point of view held by the dreamer.
Source: Jimmy Chang / Unsplash

It first popped up as a subreddit in 2021 asking about shared dream spaces. Descriptions of sprawling places resembling indoor malls were posted, with food courts, multiple levels, endless stores, and escalators. Familiar locations in waking time, in dreamtime, they appeared as strangely deserted, too crowded, or jammed with amusement parks, bathrooms, or eerie alleys of shops that meandered aimlessly.

Coined “Mall World” dreams, they share uncanny physical commonalities as well as evoke a sense of recognition, déjà-vu, and sometimes even fear or confusion. A woman posted a drawing of the mall that appears in her recurring dreams on TikTok, and it went viral, with people around the world claiming to be dreaming of a similar place.

Could we really all be dreaming of the same location? If so, what does this mean?

Location, Location, Location

Life experiences occur in places. Not just any places, but specific ones. Think about high school, for example, the primary site of our adolescence. From the sweaty anxiety of getting singled out in class to the warm feeling of belonging sitting with friends at lunch, school, as a place, is recalled not so much by name or geography but by the senses, emotions, and memories that accompany our time there.

Perceptual geographer Yi-fu Tuan writes that we know that something is real when we can apprehend it via our senses. Not just the sight of an object, but the smell, taste, touch, or sound of something. These sense-based experiences place us in both time and space. Without that physical ground, experience is abstract.

Most dreams start with a description of location. Location in dreams is a creation of the dreamer’s mind, and often an amalgam of experiences. We may dream, for example, that we are sitting in our 10th-grade science class, but our desk has our waking-time office computer sitting on it. Or, we may dream of our current house, but notice it is decorated with furniture from our childhood. Each of these settings carries its own memories and sense-based associations. Incongruously appearing together, they provoke a new perspective or understanding.

In my book The Secret Mind: Unlock the Power of Dreams to Transform Your Life, I write about something I call the "locating aspect" of images in dreams. Like waking time, dream locations place us in a specific time and space. Unlike waking time, however, because of the created aspect of these locations, they not only set the scene, but they also describe the perspective from which the “I” part of the dreamer will navigate the environment. They are the depiction of the dreamer’s physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual present-tense experiencing.

Take the office computer in the 10th-grade science class example. The feelings, memories, emotions, and sensations of what it meant to be in 10th-grade science class will shed light on the dreamer’s current waking-time experience at work. Maybe the dreamer aced science class, or maybe science class brings back the anxiety of a failed project. Everything is in the details. The feelings and the specifics of the memory—including how the dreamer responded to the situation—tell us about how the dreamer is feeling and responding in waking time.

The locating aspect gives us a window into our inner space as it is relating to how we are seeing and behaving in our waking time. Like any good map, by pinpointing where we are, we can navigate somewhere else. If a dream is presenting a scenario of seizing up in anxiety around a work project as our current point of view, we can, in waking time, choose to draw from other life experiences and shift our emotions.

A Shakespearean Question: What’s in a Mall?

I’ve had a Mall World dream, and I’ll bet you’ve had one, too. Malls are a significant feature of modern life where shopping, entertainment, eating, and socializing come together; an indoor “window to the world.” IPSOS Consumer Tracker shows that even Gen Z, the children of the internet, are still going to malls, which, they postulate, operate as a “third space” between school or work and home.

In addition, around the world, most malls somehow look the same. I’ve been in shopping malls from Phnom Pehn to Entebbe, Cedar Rapids to Warsaw, and they have been laid out in more or less the same way. While the goods in these stores may vary, they are all designed to bring a distinct sense of uniformity to the experience. The inside of a Uniqlo in Bangkok is going to feel much like the one in Paris, for example.

Given this, it’s not surprising that the Mall World dreams share similar features, or that so many people have had a Mall World dream. Malls have become cultural fixtures that, like schools, are the site of specific experiences that become part of our sense-based and emotional memories.

But what’s in a mall? It depends on how the dreamer has experienced it. For some, it represents the bright oasis of freedom that came with shopping with friends during their teenage years, while for others it’s always been a featureless nightmare. Some of my clients have been dazzled by the treasure trove of goods they discover in malls in dreams, while others have pushed against the tide of shoppers, desperate to find a way out.

Interestingly, the online group that has grown up around “Mall World’ has become a real place for people to connect over their dreaming experience. It demonstrates another truism: Dreams are both individual and collective. While the specific experiences we have are unique to us as individuals, we all share common human feelings. All of us have been dazzled at one point by abundance, overwhelmed by too many choices, anxious about presenting a project, and desiring to ace a challenge. These moments, experienced in waking or asleep, bind us together in community all over the world. You may not have the same dream I do about being in a mall, but we’ve had the same feelings, at one time or another.

item.title: Is Staying Cool Becoming a Luxury?
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Is Staying Cool Becoming a Luxury?

Consumers are increasingly buying relief from the heat, but it’s expensive.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Instead of preparing for heat early, consumers often panic-buy when hot days make sleep and work difficult.
  • When a specific need arises, consumers' attention tends to narrow to whatever promises immediate relief.
  • As heatwaves become more a part of everyday life, comfort might become a privilege not everyone can afford.

This summer has brought heatwaves to much of the world, with sweltering temperatures in North America and Europe in particular. Unlike in places that are more used to extreme heat, consumers in the United States or in Europe are struggling to adapt because their buildings and modes of transportation are not as heat-proof. As a result, consumers are trying to help themselves to some relief from the heat: Fans have sold out, cafés fill with people craving iced drinks, grocery delivery becomes more attractive, and portable air conditioners suddenly seem desirable rather than ugly.

Consumer Motivation

Although heatwaves are becoming the new normal, consumers still seem surprised each summer when they come along. Instead of preparing for heat early on by investing in fans or air conditioners, consumers panic-buy once the first really hot days make sleep and work nearly impossible. This might seem shortsighted. But it is a common consumer phenomenon that when a specific need arises (e.g., we are very hungry, or very hot), consumers' attention narrows to whatever promises immediate relief (e.g., food, a fan), leading consumers to desire the product more and think about it in much more detail. In my own work, published in 2019, with my co-author Jochim Hansen from Salzburg University, I found that consumers who feel hot consider products that bring relief in detail because the motivation is there to purchase such a product.

But what could be wrong with consumers helping themselves and buying relief when temperatures rise? The ability to do so is very unequal in society because relief from heat is expensive. Although fans are on the cheaper side of relief measures, more effective and lasting ways to purchase relief come at a cost. Yet the costs of staying cool extend beyond the price tag of a fan or an electricity bill. They also depend on where people live and the choices available to them. A well-insulated home, access to shade, nearby parks, flexible working hours, or the option to work from home all make it easier to cope with extreme heat. Others have no choice but to commute on crowded trains, work outdoors, or live in apartments that trap heat long after the sun has set. Researchers such as Antonella Mazzone and colleagues (in 2023) have begun referring to this unequal access to cooling as cooling poverty.

Comfort as a Privilege

From a consumer perspective, this raises an interesting question. Consumers are buying fans, air conditioners, or iced coffees, but more importantly, they are buying comfort. Because the more effective measures against the heat are also more expensive, thermal comfort may become a luxury. We often think of luxury as something indulgent or extravagant, such as designer handbags or first-class travel. But in a hotter world, luxury may be to sleep comfortably through the night, work productively during the day, and escape the heat when temperatures soar. As heatwaves become more and more part of everyday life, comfort itself might be becoming a privilege that not everyone can afford.

item.title: "Am I Crazy?" Understanding Out-of-Body Feelings
item.description:
Dissociation

"Am I Crazy?" Understanding Out-of-Body Feelings

Rethinking how we understand extraordinary experiences and mental health.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • The same test that screens for psychosis also captures something one in four people feel.
  • It's not always the experience that predicts distress; it's whether anyone helped the person make sense of it.
  • Distress is more likely when the experience is intense, poorly understood, or interpreted as illness.

Last year, a woman told me about a tree she'd grown drawn to on her morning walks, episodes of merging with it, her sense of self dissolving into overwhelming love and tears, then eventually a full sense of leaving her body. She began hearing a guiding inner voice, distinct from her own thoughts, that once pushed her to approach a homeless man near the tree. She started reading meaning into small coincidences, as if the world were sending her messages. At her lowest point, she considered checking herself into a psychiatric hospital, hoping medication would let her feel "normal" again.

Her experience touched several things at once—a felt merging with nature, a guiding inner voice, meaning seen in coincidence—but it was the last part, the sense of leaving her body, that eventually became the center of her fear. That's also where this piece will focus: the disembodiment feeling, and the question of what it means, clinically, when the "self" seems to leave the body.

I share her story because she is far from alone in asking the question that sits at the center of so many of these encounters: "Am I crazy?"

A question that's more common than you'd think

A disembodiment feeling—often called an out-of-body experience, and the term I'll use interchangeably here—is the sense that one's center of awareness has left the physical body. It isn't rare; it occurs in roughly 10-25 percent of the population. Yet when it happens, especially on an ongoing basis, many people quietly wonder if something has gone wrong with their mind. One of the few studies to look directly at this found, for instance, that 4 percent of experiencers felt they were going crazy during or immediately after the experience, 26 percent felt confused, 23 percent kept it a secret, and 24 percent felt upset or frightened afterward.¹

That reaction doesn't come out of nowhere. For decades, disembodiment feelings have been folded into psychiatric frameworks, discussed alongside dissociative identity disorder, schizophrenia, borderline personality disorder, depersonalization, and disorders of body ownership.

When the questionnaire becomes the problem

Some of the very instruments used to screen for dissociation or psychosis describe a disembodied feeling almost word-for-word, with no room for context or outcome. A widely used depersonalization/derealization questionnaire asks: Have you ever felt that parts of your body were disconnected from the rest of your body? That you were a "detached observer" of yourself?² If someone answers "yes" to a list like this, what have we measured? Psychosis, or simply a disembodiment feeling that a huge portion of humanity also has, at some point?

Or consider a questionnaire developed to measure body disturbances related to schizophrenia, which originally used a set of images depicting unusual bodily experiences—several of which are, unmistakably, depictions of classic disembodiment phenomenology.³ For comparison, the same instrument includes images of experiences everyone has at some point (headaches, an itch, scratching, butterflies in the stomach) implicitly presented as "normal," while the disembodiment-adjacent images sit in the pathology column.

This overlap runs straight into how dissociation is formally diagnosed. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5) defines depersonalization/derealization disorder as persistent episodes of feeling detached from one's own body, thoughts, or surroundings—a description sitting uncomfortably close to out-of-body experiences.

The DSM-5 includes three safeguards before the label is applied. First, "reality testing" must stay intact: the person retains insight that this is subjective, not an objective change in the world. (In practice: "It felt as though I left my body" reads as depersonalization; "My soul literally left my body" pushes some clinicians toward a label closer to delusion—even though the DSM-5 explicitly excludes beliefs ordinarily accepted within a person's culture or faith. However, that protection isn't always applied consistently.) Second, symptoms must cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Third, the experience can't be better explained by substance use or another condition.

Indeed, data suggest that people who report feelings of disembodiment show somewhat higher levels of dissociation and body dissatisfaction than those who haven't.⁴,⁵ My own study found a similarly complicated picture: People who'd had a disembodiment feeling showed more mental health diagnoses, more treatment history, and higher dissociation and childhood trauma.⁶ But one detail changes things: A shorter time since the first disembodiment feeling predicted greater current mental health difficulty—distress clustered near the onset, not indefinitely afterward. That points toward disruption and adaptation rather than fixed pathology; the feeling may sometimes be less the cause of difficulty than a consequence of it, or an adaptive response.

What actually predicts distress

If the presence of a disembodiment feeling doesn't predict psychological trouble on its own, what does? Research on this points to something more specific: Anxiety tends to be higher when the experience involves a loss or dissolution of one's sense of self, and when the person struggles to make sense of what happened to them.⁷ People who can't integrate or explain their experience report more anxiety and self-concept confusion—which can feel a lot like "losing it," even when nothing about their mental health has actually changed.

In other words, it's not necessarily the experience itself driving distress nearly as much as the appraisal of it—whether a person comes to understand what happened as spiritual, meaningful, neutral, or as a sign that they're losing their mind. Distress is more likely when the experience is intense, poorly understood, or interpreted as illness. Calmer, and often deeply positive, reactions tend to follow when someone finds a framework—spiritual, neutral, or otherwise—that lets the experience make sense.

None of this means disembodiment feelings can never co-occur with mental illness, but their presence alone should never be treated as evidence that someone is unwell. The better clinical questions are about suffering, context, functioning, trauma history, and integration—not simply whether someone has had an unusual experience.

I ask them because, in my inbox, I regularly hear from people carrying enormous shame around disembodiment feelings like hers, afraid to tell even those closest to them. That silence is its own kind of harm.

The woman I met last year didn't check herself into the hospital. What she needed, it turned out, wasn't medication to make the experience stop—it was language for what had already happened to her and permission to trust it. That's the frame I keep coming back to: not "Is this pathology?" but "Does this person have what they need to make sense of what they've lived through?"
